title: Why no ranking
hook: this path teaches schools in their own terms, because each has carried people across

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting each other: the quarrel at Kosambi, and three monks lifting one water pot. Your line was meeting each other. Whom did you greet? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

The town is called Kesaputta, and its people, the Kalamas, are tired. Teachers keep passing through. Each one arrives, explains his own teaching, praises it, and then picks apart everyone else's. The next one does the same, in reverse. So when the Buddha comes through, the Kalamas ask him straight out: we're confused. Which of these people is telling the truth? It's the perfect moment for him to say: me. He doesn't. Today: why no ranking.
screen: `THE KALAMAS ARE TIRED.` → `EVERY TEACHER PRAISES HIMSELF.` → `WHO IS TELLING THE TRUTH?`

segments.voice: In the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha says it makes sense that they are unsure. Then he tells them not to settle it by report, by tradition, by scripture, by clever reasoning, or by the standing of the teacher. Instead, look at what a teaching does. When you know for yourselves that something leads to greed, hatred and confusion, to harm and suffering, set it aside. When you know it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up. Test the fruit. Second, the raft. In another discourse, the Buddha compares his teaching to a raft. A man faces a wide river with danger on this side and safety on the far side. He binds a raft from sticks and grass and paddles across. Should he then carry the raft on his head forever? No. The teaching, he says, is for crossing over, not for holding on to. Third, be honest about history. Schools have argued. Some Mahayana texts used a dismissive name for other paths, Hinayana, the lesser vehicle. Theravada keeps an old book of debates, the Kathavatthu, setting out its answers to views held by other schools. Disagreement is real and long. But that's exactly why this path does what it does. It teaches each school in its own terms, the way its own teachers would explain it, and doesn't pick a winner. Fourth, the reason. Each of these schools has been a raft. Monks in Thai forests, Zen students in Kyoto, grandmothers chanting in Lhasa, families at a Korean temple: their rafts look different, and people have crossed on all of them. Ranking the rafts doesn't get anyone across. Learning how each one floats might.
screen: `TEST THE FRUIT.` · `THE RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · `THE SCHOOLS HAVE ARGUED.` · `EACH RAFT HAS CARRIED PEOPLE.` · then, large: `NO RANKING.`

segments.voice: If you'd like to try it, sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one school you've met this year that you'll probably never join. Maybe its chanting isn't your style, or its rules, or its way of sitting. That's fine. Now picture one person it has carried: a nun, a farmer, a grandmother, a teenager in a temple courtyard. See them reaching the far bank on that raft. Let yourself honor it, quietly, without needing to climb aboard. The bell holds the time.
Why no ranking. Because each school has carried people across, this path teaches every one in its own terms and picks no winner. Today's word.
Your line: no ranking. Today, when you catch yourself putting one way above another, ask instead: what does this one do for the people who use it? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 1378 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOUR DOOR AMONG THE SCHOOLS.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers point to the Kalama Sutta's test of a teaching by its fruits and the raft simile's teaching that the dhamma is for crossing over, and inter-school bodies meet without asking anyone to give up their own school.

original.note: Pali Kalama: the people of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha whom to believe.

trapdoor: what you thought: refusing to rank the schools is just being polite.

what a scholar hears: the Kalama Sutta's test by fruits, the raft simile, and honest history: Hinayana as a dismissive name and the Kathavatthu's debates.

sources.ref: Alagaddupama Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 22), the raft simile

notes: Kalama Sutta (AN 3.65) paraphrased: teachers praising their own and disparaging others; not to go by report, tradition, scripture, reasoning or the teacher's standing; test by greed, hatred, delusion, harm and welfare. Confirm.

'Some Mahayana texts used a dismissive name for other paths, Hinayana, the lesser vehicle' and 'Theravada keeps an old book of debates, the Kathavatthu, setting out where other schools went wrong': confirm fair framing; neither school is meant as the foil.
'Disagreement is real and long' is general; confirm acceptable.
Places in the teach (Thai forests, Kyoto, Lhasa, a Korean temple) are illustrative.
Original: कालाम; confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Editor: Kathavatthu described as 'setting out its answers to views held by other schools' rather than 'where other schools went wrong', so the narrator doesn't adopt one side's verdict.
